title: Ready or Not
author: Chautona Havig
hook: At twenty-two, Aggie becomes guardian to eight children. Love now asks for skills she has never had to learn.
heading: Caring before you feel ready
paragraphs: A promise to care for someone can be sincere long before we know how to keep it. That is the question behind our choice of Ready or Not. Fresh out of college, Aggie Milliken loses her sister and brother-in-law and becomes guardian to their eight children. The future she expected gives way to a household that needs her now.

Havig gives that responsibility an everyday scale: learning to manage children and a home, navigating renovations, and dealing with a grandmother who challenges Aggie's place in the family. Those practical pressures make a useful starting point for discussion. What does a grieving family need from the adult who has stepped in? How can relatives offer help without making her feel that every mistake proves she should never have accepted the role?

We picked this for readers who want to consider faith through the work of looking after people. Aggie's confidence that God has called her to this family does not supply experience she lacks. That gap gives a reading group room to talk about willingness, competence and accepting support. It also invites a more personal question: when have we needed encouragement while still learning to do something important?

This is explicitly Christian fiction, with prayer and hymns woven into Aggie's response to difficulty. Its family comedy sits alongside bereavement and the disruption children experience after losing their parents. Readers seeking a secular domestic novel should know that faith is central. Ready or Not begins the four-book Aggie's Inheritance series, making it an accessible first meeting with this family rather than a promise to resolve their entire story in one volume.
fit: Readers of Christian family fiction, church reading groups and book clubs interested in guardianship, grief and the difference between offering help and taking control. Begin with this first volume of Aggie's Inheritance.
bio: Chautona Havig writes Christian fiction from California's Mojave Desert. Her catalogue includes the interconnected Rockland stories, family fiction, mysteries and historical romance. On her website she describes encouragement in faith as a central purpose of her writing. Aggie's Inheritance is one of her suggested starting points for readers new to her work.

title: The Secretary
author: Britney King
hook: Gillian's dream job offers a dangerous bargain: how much can an employer ask once saying no no longer feels safe?
heading: When an opportunity becomes a debt
paragraphs: The unsettling part of The Secretary's premise is how ordinary the first invitation looks. Gillian Martin needs her job at Shergar Corp. Her employer pays well, offers attractive benefits and shows a personal interest in her. An invitation to dinner arrives as a simple yes-or-no choice. Then another note asks her to help conceal a murder.

That change is our reason for selecting the book. A choice made freely at the beginning can become the means by which someone claims a much larger obligation later. King's setup gives thriller readers a concrete question to argue over: at what point does gratitude for an opportunity turn into a dangerous willingness to protect the person who provided it?

Gillian's need for the job matters to that conversation. It complicates an easy judgment from outside the situation. A reading group can examine ambition and coercion together, asking what information she has, what she stands to lose and whether a powerful employer has made refusal a realistic option. The appeal lies in following those pressures into a deliberately heightened workplace nightmare.

Expect adult psychological suspense involving murder, manipulation and an unequal relationship with an employer. This is the opening volume of a two-book Secretary story in King's After Hours catalogue. We recommend it for readers interested in compromised choices and dark workplace power. Readers wanting a gentle office romance or a self-contained account of the entire duet should choose with those distinctions in mind.
fit: Adult thriller readers and discussion groups interested in workplace power, ambition and coercion. The first volume of the Secretary duet; the employer-employee attraction is part of a dangerous suspense premise.
bio: Britney King is a Texas-based author who has published psychological thrillers since 2013. Her catalogue includes the Water, New Hope, Killer and After Hours series as well as standalone books. Her fiction frequently explores obsession, control and morally complicated choices behind apparently comfortable lives.

basis: Editorial selection based on the author's published premise, biography and description of the Secretary duet. This is a recommendation note, not a full-book review.

title: Amethysts & Alchemy
author: Rachel Rener
hook: A pharmacist who draws magic from minerals must reconsider the rival she thought she understood.
heading: A gift that changes the explanation
paragraphs: Delaney Stone has built a working life around an ability she once had no explanation for: consuming minerals allows her to draw out their magic. As a pharmacist, she conceals that gift within the remedies she makes. Amethysts & Alchemy caught our attention because its fantasy begins with someone whose competence and unusual needs occupy the same life.

Her rivalry with rock-shop owner Heath Spencer gives the adventure its friction. An opportunity to visit an ancient copper mine in China places them together, and the journey challenges what Delaney believes about him. The published setup promises mineral magic, travel and a rivals-to-lovers relationship, with an emotional-support pig adding a markedly playful note.

For a reading group, the strongest opening question is about interpretation. What changes when a character discovers that an experience once explained as a problem has another meaning? Delaney's ability belongs to a fictional magic system, but the broader conversation about being understood can still matter to readers. Her changing view of Heath offers a companion question: how much of a rivalry rests on evidence, and how much on a story we keep telling ourselves?

Rener presents this as cozy romantic fantasy with neurodivergent representation. Cozy here describes the intended tone; it does not mean the romance is closed-door. Adult sexual content and the book's irreverent humour make it a different choice from an all-ages fantasy adventure. Start here for the Amethysts & Alchemy series.
fit: Adult romantasy readers who enjoy a distinctive magic system, rivals-to-lovers banter and neurodivergent characters. Best for groups comfortable discussing adult romance alongside identity and assumptions.
bio: Rachel Rener writes romantic fantasy through Lightning Conjurer Books. Her series include Gilded Blood, The Lightning Conjurer, The Bone Whisperer and Amethysts & Alchemy. Her author website describes her interest in flawed heroines, unusual magic systems and romance, and hosts her Rachel's Renergades reader community.

basis: Editorial selection based on the author's book and series information, her published romance-content guidance and reader responses. This is a recommendation note, not a full-book review.

title: Fat Dogs and French Estates: Part 1
author: Beth Haslam
hook: A search for a French estate puts a retirement dream, a marriage and two travelling dogs on the same itinerary.
heading: The dream has to survive the journey
paragraphs: It is easy to picture a different life when the picture contains only the destination. Beth Haslam's first Fat Dogs and French Estates memoir starts earlier, with the work of trying to find that place. As retirement approaches, Beth and her husband Jack plan to buy a second home with land in France. Thirteen shortlisted estates seem to offer thirteen versions of a future they might want.

The search sends them across thousands of kilometres with their two dogs. Property viewings, unfamiliar customs and eccentric owners turn a practical itinerary into a comic travel story. Beth's published introduction makes clear that this volume concerns the hunt for an estate. Readers should expect the uncertainties of getting there, rather than begin assuming the couple are already comfortably settled in their French home.

We chose it because a shared dream can reveal very different ideas of what would make life better. A couple may agree on moving yet disagree about almost everything a particular property would require. That gives book clubs something to discuss beneath the travel humour: what can we compromise on, and what do our reactions to an imperfect place reveal about the life we actually want?

The dogs keep the adventure grounded in obligations that do not disappear when people set out for a new beginning. For readers considering later-life change, that is a useful point of connection. This is a light-hearted personal memoir and the beginning of a continuing series, not a current guide to French property law or a complete account of the eventual move. Choose it for the company, the mishaps and the conversation about turning an attractive possibility into a workable life.
fit: Readers of humorous travel memoirs, animal lovers and groups discussing retirement, marriage or starting over abroad. Begin with Part 1 and continue in order for the later stages of the French estate story.
bio: Beth Haslam grew up on an estate in Wales and later ran a human-resources consultancy. Her move toward a second home in France with her husband Jack became the basis of the Fat Dogs memoirs. Her catalogue also includes Fat Dogs and Welsh Estates and animal-focused writing drawn from her life in rural France.
